title: Saturday for Mary
hook: many Catholics give Saturdays to Mary

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ember and Rogation days, quattuor tempora, the old fasts that asked God to bless the harvest. Your line was bless the fields. Did you think about where one meal came from? Day six hundred ninety-two.

Ask an older Catholic what Friday is for, and you may hear about fish. For centuries Friday was a day without meat, kept in memory of the cross, and Catholics are still asked to mark it with some small penance. Sunday belongs to the resurrection. That leaves the day in between, the one many of us spend on laundry and errands. In many Catholic homes and parishes, by an old and quiet custom, Saturday belongs to Mary.
screen: `FRIDAY: THE CROSS.` → `SUNDAY: THE RESURRECTION.` → `SATURDAY: AN OLD, QUIET CUSTOM.`

segments.voice: Nobody can point to the day this began. The custom grew slowly in the monasteries of the early Middle Ages. Alcuin of York, a scholar at Charlemagne's court around the year 800, is often credited with writing votive Masses for each day of the week, and he gave Saturday to Mary. Within a few centuries the Saturday Mass of Our Lady was common across Europe. Why Saturday? The sources don't settle it, but one answer has stuck. Think of Holy Saturday. Jesus lies in the tomb. The disciples have scattered and gone into hiding. The Gospels say almost nothing about that day. Tradition pictures Mary as the one who kept faith while everything was silent, waiting for Sunday. So every Saturday is a small echo of that waiting, the eve of every Sunday. Luke gives her a habit that fits it. After the shepherds leave Bethlehem, the Douay-Rheims says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Kept and pondered. That's a Saturday kind of faith. The custom is still in the Roman calendar. On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when no other memorial falls, a parish may keep the memorial of Saint Mary on Saturday. In 1925 Sister Lúcia, one of the three Fatima children, said Mary had asked for a devotion of five first Saturdays: confession, Communion, the rosary and fifteen minutes of meditation. Many parishes still keep it. And at home, the simplest way is the rosary, or even one decade of it. Not every Catholic does this. It's a custom, not a law. But it gives the week a shape: the cross, the waiting, the morning.
screen: `ALCUIN GIVES SATURDAY TO MARY.` · `HOLY SATURDAY: SHE KEPT FAITH.` · `A MEMORIAL STILL IN THE CALENDAR.` · `FIVE FIRST SATURDAYS.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS, PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one decade. If you pray the rosary, take it slowly now: one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, one Glory Be. Let your fingers keep count so your mind doesn't have to. If you don't pray, or don't have beads, try the shape of it another way: ten slow breaths, and with each one bring back one thing from this week you'd like to keep and ponder, the way Luke says Mary did. The bell holds the time.
votive Mass. A Mass offered for a special intention rather than the day's usual one; Alcuin of York is credited with writing one for each day, giving Saturday to Mary. Today's word.
Your line: saturday is hers. This Saturday, before the day gets busy, give it one quiet minute: a decade, or ten breaths, or one thing from the week you keep and ponder. Day six hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the rosary or a Marian prayer on Saturdays; on free Saturdays in Ordinary Time a parish may celebrate the memorial of Saint Mary on Saturday, and some keep the Fatima devotion of the five first Saturdays.

fork.reveal: the Gospels are nearly silent, but tradition pictures her keeping faith while everything was quiet. that's one reason Saturday became hers.

original.note: Latin: Saint Mary on Saturday — the name of the Saturday memorial.

trapdoor: what you thought: Saturday is just the day off.
what it means: for many Catholics it's Mary's day, an echo of Holy Saturday, the waiting before Sunday.
what a scholar hears: Alcuin's Carolingian votive Masses, the Saturday memorial in the Roman Missal, and the Fatima first Saturdays of 1925.

notes: Luke 2:19 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording: confirm exact text.
Alcuin's authorship of the weekday votive Masses including a Saturday Mass of Mary: commonly stated (e.g. Directory on Popular Piety 188); confirm attribution and date.
Holy Saturday explanation for Mary's Saturday is one of several traditional reasons; confirm framing as 'one answer'.
Saturday memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary: permitted on Saturdays in Ordinary Time with no obligatory memorial; confirm wording.

Five first Saturdays: reported by Sister Lúcia from Pontevedra, 10 December 1925; elements (confession, Communion, five decades, fifteen minutes' meditation) and Church approval status should be checked.
Etymology of sábado/sabato from Sabbath (via Latin sabbatum): confirm.
Review edit: 'locked the doors' removed from the Holy Saturday picture (teach and fork); the locked doors in John 20:19 are on Easter evening, not Saturday. Now 'scattered and gone into hiding'.

Audit (second sample): the hook's day-name etymologies (Saturn's day, sábado, sabato) used the same device as day 693's hook (domingo, domenica, dimanche); it now starts from the week's shape (Friday for the cross, Sunday for the resurrection). 'The little Easter' is left to day 693, whose carry it is.
